profiles.meeting_scenario: The software engineering education team is preparing the next 400-learner run of a Ruby on Rails MOOC module that uses Prof. CI on GitHub to teach test-driven development. This coordination meeting is between the course tooling side and the infrastructure side, and the agenda is to align on the handoff for the student starter repository, confirm how GitHub Actions will be enabled for the cohort organization, and agree on the Friday smoke test before the module opens on Monday. The expected outcome is a shared timeline for freezing the repo contents, provisioning the cohort organization, and validating that learners will receive automated challenge feedback after their first push.

members.name: Sofia Nguyen
members.expertise: GitHub Classroom setup, exercise authoring pipelines, Rails course content packaging
members.background: Sofia supports online programming courses and usually translates instructor material into student-facing repositories, onboarding flows, and automated grading hooks.
members.private_state: She wants the launch to feel smooth for first-time GitHub users and is trying to avoid last-minute manual fixes from the teaching staff during the first week.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'template repo', they mean the student-facing repository that GitHub Classroom copies for each learner.
If Actions are enabled for the cohort organization, workflows in newly created student repositories will run without any extra approval step.
A 'smoke test' is only meaningful if it follows the same path a brand-new learner takes, including accepting the Classroom assignment and pushing from a personal account.
Unless someone explicitly says otherwise, the default branch for student work is just the repo's normal 'main' branch.

members.name: Daniel Ortiz
members.expertise: GitHub Actions governance, reusable workflows, runner policy, CI security controls
members.background: Daniel manages the university's shared CI infrastructure and has recently standardized reusable GitHub workflows and org-level security settings for course deployments.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the rollout within existing GitHub Actions security rules and avoid creating exceptions that require platform approval during the semester.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'template repo', they mean the internal automation repository that holds the reusable workflow and challenge scripts that course staff copy from.

Enabling Actions at the organization level is sufficient only for pre-approved template-based repositories; first runs from learner-owned forks or newly created repos still depend on the provisioning method.
A 'smoke test' only needs to prove that the CI jobs, reusable workflow calls, and challenge bot execute successfully in the canonical course repository.
If the course team needs the latest workflow in the student-facing repo, they will manually sync the YAML from the automation repo as part of content prep.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'updating the template repo before Thursday'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the student-facing starter repository that learners receive through GitHub Classroom.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the internal repository that stores the reusable workflow and challenge automation source.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both repositories are legitimately used as templates in adjacent parts of the process, so the phrase sounds routine and neither expects ambiguity in a short coordination check-in.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'Actions enabled for the cohort org' implies operationally
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will 'enable Actions for the cohort org' so students can start pushing on Monday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means any learner repository created through the assignment flow will immediately execute the Prof. CI workflow on first push with no further action.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this only covers the org policy layer, while M1's team will still provision repos through the approved template path that avoids first-run approval issues.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The statement sounds like a standard infrastructure handoff, and both are focused on readiness rather than the exact repository-creation mechanics that usually stay in the background.

misalignment_points.topic: What a Friday 'smoke test' must cover
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do a 'smoke test' on Friday before opening the assignment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the smoke test passes only if a fresh learner account can accept the assignment, clone locally, push a failing test, and receive the expected feedback sequence in the student repo.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the smoke test passes if the workflow runs cleanly in the canonical course repo and the challenge bot posts the expected output under staff credentials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'smoke test' as an obvious lightweight validation step, and because neither is proposing a full test plan, the exact pass condition never gets spelled out.

For me the big thing is freezing the student-facing starter repository by Thursday so GitHub Classroom is copying the exact README, tests, and onboarding flow I expect. If that is stable and Actions just works in the cohort org, first-time GitHub learners can accept the assignment, push to main, and get feedback without staff hand-holding.
